questions.question: Which sequence best describes humoral adaptive immunity after appropriate B-cell activation?
choices: B cell → plasma cell → antibody production and memory B-cell formation
Neutrophil → antibody production → T-cell memory
CD8 cell → IgE production only
Erythrocyte → complement activation
questions.explanation: Activated B cells can differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies and into memory B cells that support later secondary responses.

questions.question: A virus infects a nucleated host cell. Which antigen-presentation and T-cell pairing is most directly involved in recognition of the infected cell?
choices: MHC I presenting intracellular antigen to CD8 T cells
MHC II presenting intracellular antigen to CD4 T cells
MHC I presenting antigen to B cells only
MHC II presenting antigen to neutrophils
questions.explanation: MHC I presents peptides derived from intracellular proteins to CD8 cytotoxic T cells. This is central to responses against virus-infected cells.

questions.question: A dendritic cell processes extracellular antigen and activates a helper T-cell response. Which pairing is correct?
choices: MHC II → CD4 T cell
MHC II → CD8 T cell
MHC I → plasma cell
MHC I → mast cell
questions.explanation: Professional antigen-presenting cells use MHC II to present extracellularly derived antigen to CD4 helper T cells.

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin is most closely associated with mucosal defense in respiratory and gastrointestinal secretions?
choices: IgA
IgD
IgE
IgM
questions.explanation: IgA is prominent at mucosal surfaces and in secretions, helping protect respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

questions.question: Which statement about IgM is most accurate?
choices: It is generally an early major antibody in a primary response, but isolated results require test-specific clinical interpretation
It is the only antibody that crosses the placenta
It always proves acute bacterial infection
It is the principal mediator of immediate anaphylaxis
questions.explanation: IgM is an early major antibody in a primary response. Its interpretation depends on the infection, assay, timing, and clinical context.

questions.question: A patient develops hives, wheeze, throat tightness, vomiting, and lightheadedness minutes after a medication. What is the most important FNP decision?
choices: Wait for serum testing to confirm the diagnosis
Recognize possible anaphylaxis and activate emergency management/transfer
Schedule routine allergy follow-up before treatment
Assume the symptoms are anxiety because onset was rapid
questions.explanation: This pattern is consistent with possible anaphylaxis. Airway, breathing, circulation, emergency treatment, and emergency transfer take priority; do not delay for testing.

questions.question: Why does vaccination typically produce a faster response after later exposure to the same antigen?
choices: The vaccine permanently activates neutrophils
Memory B and T cells support a faster, stronger secondary response
Passive antibodies are produced indefinitely
MHC molecules disappear
questions.explanation: Vaccination can create adaptive immune memory. Memory lymphocytes respond more rapidly and effectively on later antigen exposure.

questions.question: Which statement best describes passive immunity?
choices: The recipient produces long-term memory after receiving another person's antibodies
Antibodies are provided from another source, giving immediate but temporary protection
It only occurs after natural infection
It requires CD8 cells to become plasma cells
questions.explanation: Passive immunity supplies preformed antibodies, such as maternal IgG or administered immunoglobulin. It is immediate but does not create the recipient's adaptive memory.

questions.question: A patient receiving anti-B-cell therapy asks about a needed vaccine. Which is the safest general FNP approach?
choices: Assume every vaccine is contraindicated
Recognize possible reduced antibody response, identify vaccine type and therapy timing, and verify current guidance with the treating team when needed
Give every live vaccine immediately without reviewing medications
Tell the patient vaccines never work during immunosuppression
questions.explanation: Immune-altering therapy can affect vaccine safety or effectiveness. Medication details, vaccine type, timing, and current guidance matter; some decisions require coordination with the treating team.

questions.question: A patient has recurrent unusual infections while receiving immunosuppressive treatment. What is the most appropriate FNP reasoning?
choices: Assume repeated infections are unrelated because innate immunity is always sufficient
Review immune-altering medications, assess severity/source and host risk, pursue targeted evaluation, and escalate for serious infection
Treat each infection without medication reconciliation
Use one normal test to exclude clinically important immune dysfunction
questions.explanation: Immunosuppressive therapy can increase infection risk and alter typical presentations. A safe approach includes medication review, source/severity assessment, targeted testing, and escalation when indicated.
